title: Intro to Random Variables and Probability Distributions
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 2.8 Intro to Random Variables and Probability Distributions
intro: After this lesson you can decide whether a variable is a random variable and whether it is discrete or continuous, and build a probability distribution for a discrete random variable from the rules of probability.

moments.title: What a random variable is
moments.text: A variable whose value is a number that comes from a random process. Name it with a capital letter such as $X$.

moments.title: Four examples
moments.text: A die roll, the number of races a horse wins, seconds spent brushing teeth, and the height of a random man. Each outcome is a number.

moments.title: Words are not a random variable
moments.text: Heads or tails is only a random process. The outcome has to be a number.

moments.title: Discrete and continuous
moments.text: Discrete outcomes can be listed, usually whole-number counts. Continuous outcomes fill an interval and cannot be listed.

moments.title: Sorting examples
moments.text: Counts such as dice, wins, shirts sold, and points are discrete. Measured values such as time and height are continuous.

moments.title: Probability distribution
moments.text: Lists every possible value of a discrete random variable with its probability. The probabilities add to 1.

moments.title: Table, graph, function
moments.text: A distribution can be shown as a table, as a bar graph, or as a function. This video uses tables and graphs.

moments.title: Reading a given distribution
moments.text: Four or more shirts means adding the probabilities for 4 and 5, which gives 0.16.

moments.title: Horse races with a tree
moments.text: Conditional win chances call for a tree diagram. Multiply along each branch.

moments.title: Two branches, one value
moments.text: Win then lose, or lose then win, both give one win. Calculate each branch and add them.

moments.title: Up to three attempts
moments.text: A tree with changing probabilities. Two different branches end at three attempts, so they are added.

moments.title: Total of two plays
moments.text: List every pair of plays that gives each total, multiply for each pair, then add the pairs with the same total.

moments.title: Do not miss a value
moments.text: The instructor first forgot a total of 4. The probabilities will not sum to 1 if a value is missing.

moments.title: Lion cubs surviving
moments.text: A conditional tree gives the distribution of how many of two cubs survive.

moments.title: Difference of two players' scores
moments.text: Sasha minus Penny. List every pair of scores that gives each difference, then add their probabilities.

moments.title: Throws at a carnival game
moments.text: The player stops at the first hit or when the money runs out, so four throws has two branches.

cards.name: Discrete
cards.text: Numerical outcomes you can list, usually whole-number counts.

cards.name: Continuous
cards.text: Measured values. Any number in an interval is possible, so you cannot list them.

cards.name: Not a random variable
cards.text: The outcomes are words, such as heads or tails.

cells: Roll a die and record the number shown
Number of races a horse wins in two races
Number of T-shirts sold at a craft show
Height in inches of a randomly chosen man
Toss a coin and record heads or tails

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: Lots of possible values does not make a variable continuous. T-shirts sold could be any whole number up to 54 and is still discrete, because the values can be listed.

sections.title: Build a probability distribution
sections.intro: A horse enters two races. It wins the first race with probability 0.70. If it wins the first, it wins the second with probability 0.85. If it loses the first, it wins the second with probability 0.40. Let $W$ be the number of races it wins.
steps: List every possible value of the variable in numerical order, lowest to highest.
Find the probability of each value with the rules of probability. Draw a tree when the probabilities are conditional, and multiply along each branch.
If more than one outcome gives the same value, calculate each outcome and add them.
Check that the probabilities add to 1, then show only the final table.

parts.label: Exactly one win
parts.text: $W=1$. Two branches, so add them to get 0.225.

parts.label: Check
parts.text: A total other than 1 means a value or branch is missing.

sections.title: Write it so it earns credit

traps.title: Using one branch when several give the same value
Leaving out a possible value
traps.weak: Two plays of the game give totals of 0, 1, 2, and 3.
traps.better: A total of 4 is possible with 2 and 2. List every pair first, then check that the probabilities add to 1.

traps.title: Define the variable and use it in the statement
traps.better: Let $W$ be the number of races the horse wins. $P(W=2)=0.595$.

traps.title: Calling a long list of counts continuous
traps.weak: T-shirts sold could be anywhere from 0 to 54, so it is continuous.
traps.better: The number of T-shirts is a count of whole numbers that can be listed, so it is a discrete random variable.

traps.title: Subtracting in the wrong order
traps.weak: Penny minus Sasha when asked for Sasha minus Penny.
traps.better: Take the difference in the order the question gives. Sasha 10 and Penny 11 give $-1$ for Sasha minus Penny.

questions.stem: Which is a discrete random variable?
opts: The time in minutes a commute takes
The weight in pounds of a package
The number of red lights a driver hits on a route with 6 lights
why: Time is measured and can take any value in an interval, so it is continuous.
Weight is measured, so it is continuous.
Temperature is measured, so it is continuous.
A count of 0 to 6 that can be listed.

questions.stem: A discrete random variable $X$ has $P(0)=0.15$, $P(1)=0.35$, $P(2)=k$, and $P(3)=0.20$. What is $k$?
why: 0.70 is the sum of the other three probabilities, not what is left over.
That would make the total 1.05.
The probabilities add to 1, so $k=1-0.15-0.35-0.20=0.30$.
That is $1-0.35$, which ignores two of the other probabilities.

questions.stem: A spinner lands on 1 with probability 0.4 and on 2 with probability 0.6. It is spun twice, independently, and $T$ is the total. What is $P(T=3)$?
why: That is one ordering only, $0.4(0.6)$. A total of 3 can also come from 2 then 1.
That averages the probabilities and has no basis in the rules.
That is the total of all the probabilities.

questions.stem: A player makes the first shot with probability 0.6. After a make, the next shot is made with probability 0.7. After a miss, it is made with probability 0.5. Let $M$ be the number of makes in two shots. What is $P(M=1)$?
why: $0.6(0.3)+0.4(0.5)=0.18+0.20=0.38$. Add the make-miss and miss-make branches.
That is the make-then-miss branch only.
That is the miss-then-make branch only.
That ignores the conditional probabilities.

questions.stem: A researcher tosses a coin and records heads or tails. Why is the recorded outcome not a random variable?
opts: The coin could land on its edge
The outcomes are words, not numbers
why: Rare outcomes do not matter here. The issue is the type of outcome.
A random variable needs a numerical outcome. Heads or tails is just a random process.
Independence is not the issue.
The two outcomes can be listed easily.

sections.title: Write a full response
sections.prompt: The probability that it rains on Saturday is 0.30. If it rains on Saturday, the probability that it rains on Sunday is 0.60. If it does not rain on Saturday, the probability that it rains on Sunday is 0.20. Let $R$ be the number of rainy days on the weekend.
parts: (a) State the possible values of $R$ and whether $R$ is discrete or continuous. Explain.
(c) Find the probability that it rains on at least one day of the weekend.
sample: (a) $R=0, 1, 2$. $R$ is discrete because it counts days, so the values can be listed.
checklist: (a) Lists 0, 1, 2 and says discrete with a reason
(b) Uses the tree and multiplies along branches
(b) Adds the two branches that give $R=1$
(b) Final table with all three values and probabilities that add to 1
(c) Adds $P(R=1)$ and $P(R=2)$ or uses the complement, with the event in context
